## Droughts - A Working Definition

Drought has no single, universally accepted definition, and which one applies depends on the part of the water cycle and the impacts under consideration [@zargarReviewDroughtIndices2011].
Four types are commonly distinguished, better understood as sequential stages of one process than as independent categories (Figure \@ref(fig:drought-types), adapted from @nandgudeDroughtPredictionComprehensive2023): a precipitation deficit produces a *meteorological* drought, which depletes soil moisture into an *agricultural* drought, lowers streamflow and groundwater into a *hydrological* drought, and finally reaches water-dependent goods as a *socioeconomic* drought.

```{r drought-types, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="The four drought types as a propagating cascade, adapted from @nandgudeDroughtPredictionComprehensive2023.", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/figures/general/drought_types_vector.svg")
```

This work targets meteorological drought, the first stage and earliest signal, driven by a precipitation deficit together with high evapotranspiration.
It is quantified with standardized indices, of which this work uses the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) [@vicente-serranoMultiscalarDroughtIndex2010]. 
SPEI extends the precipitation-only Standardized Precipitation Index [@mckeeRelationshipDroughtFrequency1993] by using the water balance, so that temperature enters through evapotranspiration, which can account more for rising temperatures under climate change.

The SPEI is built on the monthly climatic water balance,

$$D = P - PET, \qquad \begin{cases} D > 0 & \text{water surplus} \\ D < 0 & \text{water deficit} \end{cases}$$

where $P$ is precipitation and $PET$ is potential evapotranspiration.

For each grid cell the water balance is accumulated over the chosen timescale, fitted to a distribution, and transformed to a standard normal, so that the resulting SPEI is expressed in standard deviations from the local mean.
It is computed as in @funk2026probabilisticdeeplearningdrought, with a three-parameter gamma fit calibrated over 1990 to 2019.

## Related Work

Beyond simple baselines such as logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees [@marusovLongtermDroughtPrediction2024a], drought prediction has increasingly turned to machine learning and deep learning [@nandgudeDroughtPredictionComprehensive2023]. The drought prediction task poses two intertwined challenges.
It is temporal, since a future drought has to be inferred from a history of past conditions, which calls for models that handle sequential data. 
It is also spatial, since the data are gridded or measured at related locations, so nearby places are not independent. 
How a model treats these two aspects, and how well it handles each, is what mainly separates the approaches below.

One way to handle the temporal side is the LSTM. 
In its basic form it predicts a drought index from a sequence of past features [@wangDroughtPredictionInsights2023]. 
Other designs extend it, for example folding in nearby stations through a temporal-convolution and attention hybrid [@chenSTATLSTMMultivariateSpatiotemporal2025]. 
Either way, these models capture temporal dependencies well but handle space only through the inputs rather than modeling the field jointly.

Other work models space more directly. 
Graph-based approaches treat grid points as nodes and aggregate over neighbors before a recurrent temporal module, for example a GraphSAGE encoder followed by a GRU with self-attention [@yuMultivariateSpatiotemporalModeling2023]. 
Transformer and foundation models bring spatial forecasting over from weather and climate, including EarthFormer [@gaoEarthformerExploringSpaceTime2023], FourCastNet [@pathakFourCastNetGlobalDatadriven2022], and the Vision-Transformer foundation model ClimaX, pretrained on large climate-simulation archives [@nguyenClimaXFoundationModel2023]. 
These are powerful but designed for large-scale, often global data and substantial compute, and their advantage over simpler models is not guaranteed, since a simple linear baseline can match or outperform transformer forecasters on standard time-series benchmarks [@zengAreTransformersEffective2022].

These approaches share some tendencies, at least among the studies considered here.
They mostly forecast at a short lead, typically one month ahead [@wangDroughtPredictionInsights2023; @chenSTATLSTMMultivariateSpatiotemporal2025; @yuMultivariateSpatiotemporalModeling2023],
the exception being a twelve-month horizon reached by treating drought as a binary classification over global regions [@marusovLongtermDroughtPrediction2024a]. 
Their evaluation usually falls on one side of a divide, either a continuous index scored by average error such as RMSE [@wangDroughtPredictionInsights2023; @chenSTATLSTMMultivariateSpatiotemporal2025]
or discrete drought categories scored by typical classification evaluation metrics such as the F1-score [@yuMultivariateSpatiotemporalModeling2023], rather than a continuous field judged for both accuracy and severe-event detection. 
And in these studies the loss function and the handling of input features are left at a single approach rather than compared across different approaches.

This work predicts the continuous SPEI as a spatial field at a twelve-month lead over the Alps, evaluates it for both point accuracy and severe-drought detection,
and, above all, studies how the loss and the conditioning on global and static features shape the trade-off between the two.

## Data and Task

### Domain and source

The study region is the Alpine domain at monthly resolution from 1971 to 2024 (648 months).
The data is derived from the ERA5-Land reanalysis, regridded to this grid and provided in preprocessed form.
SPEI was supplied already computed, following @funk2026probabilisticdeeplearningdrought.
A fixed mask marks the valid Alpine cells, shown outlined against the surrounding European topography in Figure \@ref(fig:al-topography).

```{r al-topography, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Topography over Europe. The red outline marks the Alpine study domain used in this work.", out.width="70%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/figures/raw/topography.svg")
```

### Variables

The inputs fall into three groups.

*Dynamic spatial* variables vary in space and time: SPEI (the target, also supplied as history), precipitation, near-surface temperature, surface pressure, and the climatic water balance (precipitation minus potential evapotranspiration).
Together these capture the local water supply and demand and the large-scale circulation that drive meteorological drought.
Figure \@ref(fig:spei-snapshots) shows SPEI, the most directly drought-relevant of these, across a sequence of months.

*Dynamic global* variables vary in time only: the North Atlantic Oscillation index [@nao_TODO], grouped Mediterranean sea-surface temperatures, and a cyclical month encoding.
These capture large-scale drivers of European moisture and its seasonality, with the fourteen Mediterranean basins grouped into three regional means (western Mediterranean, eastern Mediterranean, Black Sea) [@millotCirculationMediterraneanSea2005; @lionelloMediterraneanClimateOverview2006], shown in Figure \@ref(fig:med-slt).

*Static spatial* variables vary in space only: the topography, since Alpine elevation strongly shapes precipitation and temperature.

```{r spei-snapshots, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Raw SPEI over the Alpine domain across a sequence of months, illustrating the spatial and temporal variability the model has to capture.", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/figures/raw/al/spei.svg")
```

```{r med-slt, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Mediterranean SLT, 1971--2024, aggregated into the same three regional groups (western Mediterranean, eastern Mediterranean, Black Sea) used as global scalar model input.", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/figures/raw/slides/mediterranean_slt.svg")
```

### Preprocessing

Cells outside the Alpine mask are filled and excluded from all statistics.
All variables, including SPEI, are standardized to zero mean and unit variance using statistics from the training years and valid cells only, so that every input shares a common scale and the normalization draws on no information beyond the training period.
SPEI, supplied on its own 1990 to 2019 reference, is thereby brought onto the same training-period footing as the other variables.

### Split and nonstationarity

The data are split chronologically to prevent look-ahead leakage: training on 1971 to 2004, validation on 2005 to 2014, and testing on 2015 to 2024.
Because the split is by time rather than at random, the periods differ in climate.
The average severe-drought frequency rises across them, from 0.53 to 0.62 to 1.04 events per cell per year, so the test period is both out of sample and drier than the training period, as shown per cell in Figure \@ref(fig:drought-freq-severe).

```{r drought-freq-severe, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Per-cell severe-drought (SPEI $\\le -1.5$) frequency by split. The rightward shift from train to test is why the periods are treated as climatically different rather than identically distributed.", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/figures/processed/exploratory/drought_frequency_severe.svg")
```

### Task

The forecasting task is a continuous, per-cell regression of SPEI.
Given thirty-six months of history, the model predicts a single SPEI map at a twelve-month lead, the field for the month one year after the input window.
The forecast is direct rather than recursive: the target horizon is predicted in one step instead of iterating month by month, which avoids the error accumulation of recursive forecasting.

## Model

The forecasting model is a Convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM), following the variant of @marusovLongtermDroughtPrediction2024a.
It replaces the matrix products in the gates of a standard LSTM [@PDFLongShortTerm] with convolutions, so the input $x_t$, hidden state $h_t$, and cell state $c_t$ are three-dimensional feature maps rather than vectors, which preserves spatial structure and models spatial and temporal dependencies jointly.
Figure \@ref(fig:convlstm-schematic) shows the resulting cell.

```{r convlstm-schematic, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="ConvLSTM cell: every gate is a 2D convolution over the concatenated input and hidden-state feature maps, so $x_t$, $h_t$, and $c_t$ stay spatial feature maps throughout.", out.width="75%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/figures/architecture/ConvLSTM.svg")
```

Each gate applies a convolution followed by batch normalization, whose affine shift replaces the additive bias,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_t &= \sigma(\mathrm{BN}(W_f \ast x_t + U_f \ast h_{t-1})), & i_t &= \sigma(\mathrm{BN}(W_i \ast x_t + U_i \ast h_{t-1})), \\
\tilde{c}_t &= \tanh(\mathrm{BN}(W_c \ast x_t + U_c \ast h_{t-1})), & o_t &= \sigma(\mathrm{BN}(W_o \ast x_t + U_o \ast h_{t-1})),
\end{aligned}
$$

and the cell and hidden states are updated as

$$c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t, \qquad h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t),$$

where $\ast$ denotes convolution, $\odot$ the elementwise product, and $\sigma$ the sigmoid.

The final hidden state is mapped to the predicted SPEI field by a bounded regression head,

$$\hat{y}_T = \lambda \tanh(W_{\text{out}} \ast h_T),$$

where the scaled $\tanh$ keeps the output within $[-\lambda, \lambda]$, with $\lambda = 10$.

## Methods

The experiments address the three questions from the introduction: how the loss function shapes the trade-off between point accuracy and drought detection (RQ1), how dynamic global features are best integrated into the ConvLSTM (RQ2), and how static spatial features are best integrated (RQ3).
Each is treated as one axis of variation, defined below.

### RQ1: Loss functions

The loss determines how strongly errors on dry cells are weighted relative to the rest, and so how hard the model is pushed to predict droughts.
Three families are compared, each averaged over valid cells, with $y$ the observed and $\hat{y}$ the predicted (standardized) SPEI.

<div style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 380px; align-items: center; gap: 1.5em;">
<div style="min-width: 0;">

*Mean squared error* is the symmetric baseline,

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = (\hat{y} - y)^2.$$

</div>
<div style="min-width: 0; width: 380px; text-align: right;">
```{r mse-illustration, echo=FALSE, out.width="170px", fig.cap="MSE loss."}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/reports/figures/mse.svg")
```
</div>
</div>

<div style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 380px; align-items: center; gap: 1.5em;">
<div style="min-width: 0;">

*Hinge-weighted MSE* keeps the squared error but up-weights cells on the dry side of normal,

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\text{hwMSE}} &= w\,(\hat{y} - y)^2, \\
w &= 1 + \alpha \max(0, -y), \quad \alpha \in \{1, 5\},
\end{aligned}$$

so a given error costs more the drier the observed cell.

</div>
<div style="min-width: 0; width: 380px; text-align: right;">
```{r hinge-illustration, echo=FALSE, out.width=c("170px","170px"), fig.show="hold", fig.cap="Hinge weight $w(y)$ (left) and the resulting weighted MSE (right)."}
knitr::include_graphics(c(
  "work/02-drought_prediction/reports/figures/hinge_weight.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/reports/figures/hinge_loss.svg"
))
```
</div>
</div>

<div style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 380px; align-items: center; gap: 1.5em;">
<div style="min-width: 0;">

*Pinball (quantile) loss* at $\tau = 0.20$ is asymmetric,

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{pin}} = \begin{cases} \tau\,(y - \hat{y}) & \hat{y} \le y, \\ (1-\tau)\,(\hat{y} - y) & \hat{y} > y, \end{cases}$$

penalizing over-prediction, that is predicting too wet and so missing a drought, by a factor $\tfrac{1-\tau}{\tau} = 4$ more than under-prediction, which biases the model toward the dry tail.

</div>
<div style="min-width: 0; width: 380px; text-align: right;">
```{r pinball-illustration, echo=FALSE, out.width="170px", fig.cap="Pinball loss at $\\tau=0.20$."}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/reports/figures/pinball.svg")
```
</div>
</div>

### RQ2: Dynamic global features
Two ways of feeding the global features (NAO, Mediterranean SST, month) into the ConvLSTM are compared, contrasted in Figure \@ref(fig:naive-vs-film).
The naive baseline (left) broadcasts each global scalar across the spatial grid and appends it as an extra input channel.

```{r naive-vs-film, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Naive injection (left) broadcasts each global scalar across the grid and appends it as an input channel. FiLM (right) instead uses the global features to produce a per-channel scale $\\gamma_{t,c}$ and shift $\\beta_{t,c}$ applied to the embedding.", out.width="90%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/figures/architecture/Naive_vs_film.svg")
```

FiLM (feature-wise linear modulation) [@perezFiLMVisualReasoning2018] (right) instead conditions the network by applying a per-channel affine transform to the feature maps,

$$\mathrm{FiLM}(F_c) = \gamma_c\, F_c + \beta_c, \qquad \gamma_c = f_c(x_t), \; \beta_c = h_c(x_t),$$

where $F_c$ is the activation of channel $c$ and the scale $\gamma_c$ and shift $\beta_c$ are learned functions $f_c, h_c$ of the global features $x_t$.
Rather than adding channels, FiLM lets the global state reshape the existing ones. Figure \@ref(fig:convlstm-film) shows where this conditioning enters the ConvLSTM cell introduced above.

```{r convlstm-film, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Where FiLM sits inside the ConvLSTM cell: it conditions the embedded input feature map before the gate convolutions.", out.width="75%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/figures/architecture/ConvLSTM_FiLM.svg")
```

### RQ3: Static spatial features
Three ways of incorporating the static topography are compared, contrasted in Figure \@ref(fig:naive-vs-static-encoder).
The naive baseline (left) appends the raw static field repeateadly at each time step, treating it the same as a dynamic spacial feature.

```{r naive-vs-static-encoder, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Naive injection (left) appends the raw static field as constant channels. The learned encoder (right) instead passes it through a small CNN -- one shared convolution for \\emph{single}, or four season-selected convolutions for \\emph{seasonal} -- before concatenating the result.", out.width="90%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/figures/architecture/Naive_vs_single_seasonal.svg")
```

The other two learn a seperate static encoding through a small convolutional network,

$$E(S) = \mathrm{ReLU}(W_2 \ast \mathrm{ReLU}(W_1 \ast S)),$$

with static features $S$ and convolutional kernels $W_1, W_2$ (each with batch normalization), whose output is concatenated to the embedding $x_t^{\text{emb}}$ at every timestep.
The *single* variant uses one shared encoder, giving $[\,x_t^{\text{emb}}, E(S)\,]$, while the *seasonal* variant uses four encoders, one per meteorological season, selected by the season $s(m_t)$ of the target month, giving $[\,x_t^{\text{emb}}, E_{s(m_t)}(S)\,]$. Figure \@ref(fig:convlstm-static) shows where the resulting encoder output enters the cell.

```{r convlstm-static, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Where the static encoder sits inside the ConvLSTM cell: its output is concatenated to the embedded input and hidden state before the gate convolutions.", out.width="75%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/02-drought_prediction/figures/architecture/ConvLSTM_static.svg")
```

### Experimental setup

The three axes are crossed into a full grid of $4 \times 2 \times 3 = 24$ configurations: four losses, by two global-feature strategies, by three static-feature strategies.
All configurations share the chronological split above, a single random seed (42), and the same training protocol: the Adam optimizer with batch size 32, up to 50 epochs with early stopping on the validation RMSE, and the learning rate reduced on plateau.

### Evaluation

All metrics are computed on the test period (2015 to 2024), over the valid cells and test months.
Point accuracy is measured by the RMSE of the predicted SPEI,

$$\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T G}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\left(\hat{y}_{g,t} - y_{g,t}\right)^2},$$

over $T$ test months and $G$ valid cells.
Detection is evaluated at the severe-drought cutoff SPEI $\le -1.5$: predictions and observations are binarized at this threshold, and the true positive rate (recall) and F1 score summarize how well severe droughts are caught,

$$\mathrm{TPR} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}, \qquad \mathrm{F1} = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN}.$$

### Feature importance

Occlusion ablation quantifies model reliance by zeroing one input at a time
at evaluation time and re-scoring the frozen model, rather than permuting it,
since the driver fields are spatially and temporally correlated.
Figure \@ref(fig:feature-importance) reports the resulting $\Delta$RMSE and
$\Delta$drought-F1 for all six architecture conditions under the Pinball
loss. Point accuracy is essentially unmovable throughout
($|\Delta\text{RMSE}| < 0.06$), while detection swings by up to $0.45$:
Mediterranean SST is consistently the single most relied-upon feature, and
its ablation collapses detection entirely whenever no learned static
encoder is present, but only partially otherwise -- the same
architecture-conditional pattern recurs in the FiLM counterfactual below.

```{r feature-importance, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Occlusion feature importance, Pinball loss, all six architecture conditions ($\\Delta$RMSE left, $\\Delta$drought-F1 right, per panel). Point accuracy is essentially unmovable ($|\\Delta\\text{RMSE}| < 0.06$ throughout) while detection swings by up to 0.45; Mediterranean SST is the top detection feature in every condition, and its ablation collapses detection entirely wherever no learned static encoder is present.", out.width="48%", fig.show="hold", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(c(
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/feature_importance/naive_naive.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/feature_importance/naive_film.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/feature_importance/single_naive.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/feature_importance/single_film.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/feature_importance/seasonal_naive.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/feature_importance/seasonal_film.svg"
))
```

### Does FiLM benefit the extremes?

Figure \@ref(fig:film-stratified) breaks RMSE and mean bias down by
observed-SPEI bin for naive/naive against naive/film and seasonal/film,
separately per loss. Pinball shows the cleanest extremes-only gain from
FiLM: aggregate RMSE moves by only $+0.5\%$ while the driest bin
($\text{SPEI} \le -2$) improves by $-0.10$. MSE tells a different story --
its severe dry-tail under-prediction bias ($+0.9$ to $+1.4$) is barely
moved by FiLM at all, consistent with MSE optimizing for the bulk of the
distribution rather than the tail. Figure \@ref(fig:film-case-study) grounds
this in a single worked example: the worst Alpine month of the 2022 test
year, independently selected by all four losses as July 2022
(domain-mean observed SPEI $-1.61$), shown alongside the global driver
state -- NAO and Mediterranean SST -- that FiLM conditions on for that
month.

```{r film-stratified, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="RMSE and mean bias (pred $-$ obs) by observed-SPEI bin, naive/naive vs. naive/film vs. seasonal/film, per loss. Pinball shows the cleanest extremes-only gain from FiLM (aggregate RMSE +0.5\\%, $\\le\\!-2$ bin RMSE $-0.10$); MSE's severe dry-tail under-prediction bias ($+0.9$ to $+1.4$) is barely moved by FiLM.", out.width="48%", fig.show="hold", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(c(
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/mse_stratified.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/pinball_q0.20_stratified.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/wmse_w1_hinge_stratified.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/wmse_w5_hinge_stratified.svg"
))
```

```{r film-case-study, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Worked example: the worst Alpine month in the 2022 test year (all four losses independently select July 2022, domain-mean observed SPEI $-1.61$) -- observed SPEI, naive/naive and naive/film predictions and their error maps, and the global driver state (NAO, Mediterranean SST) FiLM conditioned on.", out.width="48%", fig.show="hold", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(c(
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/mse_2022_case_study.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/pinball_q0.20_2022_case_study.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/wmse_w1_hinge_2022_case_study.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/wmse_w5_hinge_2022_case_study.svg"

```

A stratified breakdown shows FiLM's effect but not whether the model is
actually using the global scalars it is conditioned on, versus using them
for a marginal correction on top of some other, more informative pathway.
Figure \@ref(fig:film-counterfactual) tests this directly with a
counterfactual: zeroing the global scalars at evaluation time and measuring
the relative change in extreme-bin ($\text{SPEI} \le -1.5$) RMSE against the
true-scalar baseline. naive/film collapses by $62$--$118\%$ once the
scalars are removed, confirming it genuinely depends on them for extreme
prediction; seasonal/film, which has an alternative spatial pathway into the
static encoder, degrades by only $11$--$34\%$ -- the same
architecture-conditional reliance pattern already seen in the feature
importance results above.

```{r film-counterfactual, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Genuineness counterfactual: relative change in extreme-bin (SPEI $\\le -1.5$) RMSE when the global scalars are zeroed vs. their true values, naive/film vs. seasonal/film, per loss. naive/film collapses by 62--118\\%; seasonal/film, which has an alternative spatial pathway, by only 11--34\\% -- the same architecture-conditional pattern found in the feature-importance results.", out.width="48%", fig.show="hold", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(c(
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/mse_counterfactual.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/pinball_q0.20_counterfactual.svg",
  "work/02-drought_prediction/figures/interpretability/film_extremes/wmse_w1_hinge_counterfactual.svg",

))
```
